paras: The expulsion of Black hotel workers from Holdenville, Indian Territory, took place in late January 1903, when a dynamite bomb was thrown at the quarters of Black hotel help who had been ordered to leave the town. No one was reported hurt, but the workers left on the first outgoing train. Papers in Kansas and Indian Territory reported it as a case of a town enforcing a rule that no Black people should live there.

According to a Holdenville dispatch in the Daily Ardmoreite, the town held to an "unwritten law" that "no negroes shall live here," though the need for domestics and hotel help had led to the employment of a few Black workers. When several hotels hired Black help, local sentiment turned at once against the hotel keepers, and the workers were ordered to leave town but did not go. The Ardmoreite added that "dire threats" had been made against both the Black workers and those who employed them.

About 11 o'clock on Saturday night, January 24, someone threw a dynamite bomb at a small building behind one of the hotels that served as servants' quarters. The Wichita Daily Eagle's correspondent attributed it to "some miscreant" acting "to frighten them away," while the Ardmoreite described an "outbreak" in which the quarters of the Hotel Scott were dynamited. The blast smashed windows and caused a "stampede" of the workers, who left on the first train out of town.

Because an armed posse had guarded the Frisco train through town that evening against a feared hold-up, many residents took the explosion for a robbery and ran with revolvers and Winchesters to the bank, which they found untouched.

No arrest or investigation for the bombing appears in the coverage. On the following day a party of Black domestic girls was accosted on the street, and the man accused was tried on Tuesday in the commissioner's court on a charge of using vile and indecent language; no verdict was reported. The Ardmoreite reported that a number of the town's leading men backed that prosecution and had decided to defend their domestic help "despite the violent opposition of the community."

The Wichita Daily Eagle ran the Holdenville dispatch on its front page under the headline "Dynamite Frightens Negroes," and closed with the town's relief that the worst damage was "the loss of the negro help and a few broken window glasses." The same paper's "Outlines of Oklahoma" column condensed the story to a quip that the workers "went a-flying," and the Chickasha Daily Express reprinted that item two days later.

The Daily Ardmoreite headlined its account "Serious Race Trouble" and described bitter feeling in the town, yet ended by asserting that the matter was "not a question of race, but a question of competent domestic help." By February 7 the story had reached the St. Landry Clarion in Louisiana as a two-sentence brief stating that "the homes of the colored people" had been dynamited. All of these reports appeared in white papers, and no Black-press account of the January 1903 bombing appears in the coverage.

The accounts differ on scale: the Eagle described one bomb at a single servants' building and "a few" broken windows, while the Ardmoreite called the explosion "terrific," rocking many buildings in the business section. The Clarion's later reference to dynamited "homes," in the plural, is not supported by either Holdenville dispatch, both of which describe workers' quarters at a hotel.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black hotel workers from Holdenville, Indian Territory (1903)
bases: Black hotel workers were ordered to leave town, and when they did not, a dynamite bomb was thrown at their quarters 'in order to frighten them away' and they left on the first train (A1, A2, A3).

Two separately worded Holdenville dispatches dated Jan. 28 and Jan. 29 (A1, A3) agree on the order to leave, the Saturday-night dynamiting of the workers' quarters behind a hotel and the workers' departure by train; A2 and A5 are condensed briefs.

accounts.label: Wichita Eagle Holdenville dispatch (Jan. 28)
accounts.gist: A lone 'miscreant' threw a bomb against the servants' quarters to frighten the workers, who had refused an order to leave; the blast broke windows and the workers left by train.

accounts.label: Daily Ardmoreite Holdenville dispatch (Jan. 29)
accounts.gist: Town sentiment under an 'unwritten law' against Black residents erupted in the dynamiting of the Hotel Scott's quarters; the explosion rocked the business section and the workers fled.

accounts.label: Later condensed brief
accounts.gist: Holdenville citizens trying to enforce a rule that no Black people live there dynamited 'the homes of the colored people'.

Column item treats the expulsion lightly: 'they went a-flying'.
